text:
**The Ultimate Test for Entrepreneurs: 5 Signs You've Achieved Early Product-Market Fit**

 Ah, product-market fit – that elusive holy grail every entrepreneur strives to attain. It's the moment when your solution solves real problems for real customers, and they can't get enough of it.

As someone who's been through this journey myself with EchoSign (now DocuSign), I know firsthand how exhilarating it feels when you finally achieve early product-market fit. But here's the thing: it's not just about feeling good; it's about executing on a scalable business model that will propel you towards growth and success.

So, how do you know if you've achieved early product-market fit? Look out for these five telltale signs:

 **1. Your Customers Are Using Your Solution Regularly**

It's one thing to have users sign up for your platform or app, but it's another story altogether when those same users come back day after day, week after week. If you're seeing consistent engagement from your customer base, it's likely a sign that you're solving a genuine problem that resonates with them.

At EchoSign, we saw our users check their accounts multiple times per day, often to see if new documents had been uploaded or to review pending signatures. This level of engagement told us that we were onto something big.

 **2. Customer Acquisition Costs are Decreasing Over Time**

When you first launch, acquiring customers is expensive – think Google Ads, content marketing, and referral programs galore. However, as you refine your value proposition and improve user experience, costs should naturally decrease over time.

We found that at EchoSign, once we'd established a solid product-market fit, our customer acquisition costs plummeted by more than half compared to our earlier days. That was music to my ears!

 **3. Positive Word-of-Mouth Spreads Like Wildfire**

There's no better endorsement than an existing customer referring friends, family, and colleagues to your solution. When word-of-mouth spreads rapidly, it indicates that people genuinely love what you offer and want others to benefit from it too.

During EchoSign's heyday, referrals accounted for nearly 50% of our new sign-ups. Talk about social proof!

 **4. Competitors Start to Take Notice**

Product-market fit isn't just about beating internal metrics; it also means attracting external attention. As you establish yourself as a leader in your space, competitors will start taking notice and trying to replicate your success.

At EchoSign, we noticed that other e-signature companies began emulating some of our features, which only reinforced our confidence in our approach.

 **5. Revenue Growth Accelerates Exponentially**

Let's face it: revenue growth is the lifeblood of any successful startup. And when you've achieved early product-market fit, expect your top-line numbers to accelerate exponentially as you scale your sales efforts.

For EchoSign, revenue grew at an average rate of 200% YoY during our most successful periods. Those kinds of numbers don't happen by accident – they require a deep understanding of your market and a commitment to delivering exceptional results.

In conclusion, achieving early product-market fit requires dedication, perseverance, and a willingness to adapt to changing circumstances. By looking for these five telltale signs, you'll be well-equipped to identify whether you're on the right path or need to pivot your strategy.

Remember, getting to early product-market fit takes time, effort, and resources. Don't give up! With persistence and a clear vision, you'll unlock the potential for explosive growth and build a lasting legacy in the process.

topic: 5 Reasons to Actually Have Board Meetings
prompt: Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: 5 Reasons to Actually Have Board Meetings
text:
**The Surprising Truth About Board Meetings**

As I sit here writing this, I'm reminded of my early days as an entrepreneur. We thought board meetings were a waste of time - just another unnecessary hurdle to get over on our way to growth and success.

But let me tell you, that was wrong.

In fact, having regular board meetings is one of the most important things we did at EchoSign (now DocuSign). It kept us accountable, helped us make tough decisions, and ultimately drove our company's massive growth.

So what are some reasons why your startup should actually have board meetings? Here are five:

### Reason #1: Accountability

Having a board can be scary, especially if you're used to being the sole decision-maker in your company. But trust me, it's worth it. A good board will hold you accountable for your actions, and keep you focused on the goals that really matter. They'll ask the hard questions, like "What's the plan?" or "How do you intend to execute?"

I remember when we first started holding board meetings at EchoSign. Our board members would grill me with questions, pushing me to think more critically about our business model and strategy. At first, it was uncomfortable. But soon enough, those sessions became invaluable. We got better, faster, because someone else was watching over us.

### Reason #2: Objectivity

Your team might love you, but they also tend to see the world through rose-tinted glasses. That's natural - after all, you've invested countless hours into building something amazing! However, outside perspectives are essential for evaluating your progress, spotting blind spots, and making informed decisions.

Our board brought expertise from various industries, which helped us navigate complex challenges and stay ahead of competitors. For instance, our CFO had experience leading large-scale financial transactions; his input saved us millions during our Series C round.

### Reason #3: Networking Opportunities

A strong board network opens doors to new connections, partnerships, and potential hires. When you surround yourself with experienced entrepreneurs, investors, and industry leaders, opportunities start flowing in. This not only accelerates growth but also expands your knowledge base, allowing you to tackle increasingly difficult problems.

One of our board members introduced us to a key client who ended up becoming one of our biggest partners. Another led us to a top talent who joined our leadership team shortly thereafter.

### Reason #4: Access to Capital

Let's face it: raising capital can be brutal, especially for startups. Having a solid board relationship gives you credibility with VCs, angels, and other investors. Your board members often have existing relationships within these communities, which can help grease the wheels when fundraising.

During our last funding round, our board chairman made several introductions to influential LPs, which smoothed out our process significantly.

### Reason #5: Future-Proofing

Lastly, a well-functioning board helps ensure continuity beyond your own tenure. Who knows what happens next year? Maybe you want to take a break, step down as CEO, or even sell the company. Whatever the reason, your board provides a clear path forward, ensuring that the organization remains stable and grows despite changes in leadership.

When I left DocuSign, our board played a critical role in navigating the transition period and keeping employees engaged. Their guidance allowed the company to continue thriving under its new management structure.

In conclusion, don't view board meetings as a necessary evil or a burden on your precious time. Instead, consider them a vital component of your startup's growth engine. By embracing accountability, objectivity, networking opportunities, access to capital, and future-proofing, you'll set yourself up for long-term success.

And hey, who knows - maybe one day you'll look back on your own board meetings as the turning point

**What Makes a Great VP of Marketing in SaaS?**

As I've spoken to countless VPs of Marketing across the globe, one thing has become crystal clear – there's no one-size-fits-all approach when it comes to leading marketing teams. But what sets truly great VPs apart from their peers?

To get some insights on this topic, I sat down (virtually) with my friend Dave Gerhardt, former VP of Marketing at Drift. If you're not familiar with Dave, let me tell you - he's been instrumental in building some of the most recognizable brands in the world.

**The Interview Begins...**

Jason: Hey, Dave! Thanks for joining me today. I know your background is steeped in growth hacking and brand-building. Can you give us an idea of what makes a great VP of Marketing in SaaS?

Dave: Well, first off, I think we need to redefine what 'great' means. In my opinion, a great VP of Marketing isn't just someone who churns out sales numbers; they should be driving alignment between product, sales, and customer success teams. They must understand how all these functions impact each other.

Jason: That's so spot-on. And it starts with leadership. What kind of qualities do you look for in a potential candidate for a top-marketing role?

Dave: Leadership-wise, I'm looking for someone who can inspire their team to push boundaries, experiment, and take calculated risks. This person needs to have a deep understanding of both the business and the market landscape, which allows them to make informed decisions that drive results.

**Beyond Leadership Skills**

Jason: Alright, got it. So now that we have our leadership checklist ticked off, let's talk about more tangible skills. How important are content creation, social media management, SEO optimization, etc., in the grand scheme of things?

Dave: Honestly, those individual skills are table stakes. While having expertise in areas like these will certainly help, a true leader will surround themselves with talented individuals who excel in specific domains. It's about empowering your team members to own their craft while focusing on strategy and vision-setting as the CEO or founder would.

Jason: Now I want to pivot slightly to something near and dear to many marketers' hearts: metrics. As a marketer, where should your focus lie?

Dave: Here's the thing – every metric matters, but if you only focus on vanity metrics (likes, shares, website traffic), you'll never reach scale. Your goal should always be tied back to revenue growth, conversion rates, or pipeline velocity. Make sure everyone under you understands why they're working towards a particular objective.

**Tying Everything Together**

Jason: Last question before we wrap up: What advice would you give aspiring VPs of Marketing out there who are trying to rise through the ranks?

Dave: My final piece of advice is simple yet crucial: build relationships within the organization. Build trust with your CEO, Sales leaders, Customer Success reps, and cross-functional stakeholders alike. Establish credibility by consistently delivering value-driven outcomes. Don't be afraid to take calculated risks and challenge assumptions along the way.

There you have it – actionable insights from two people who have walked the walk. Whether you're currently serving as a VP of Marketing or aspire to be one someday, remember that success lies at the intersection of leadership, vision, and adaptability.

**Takeaways:**

* Aligning multiple departments around shared goals is key.
* Surround yourself with talent rather than being an expert in everything.
* Metrics matter, especially those tied directly to revenue growth.
* Focus on establishing trust and credibility throughout the org.

If you'd like to share any additional thoughts or insights from your own experiences, please hit reply below!

Thanks again, Dave, for sharing your time and wisdom.

**The Mediocre Recycled: How to Spot and Avoid the Zombie Executives of B2B**

As I've spent years scaling SaaStr companies, I've noticed a peculiar phenomenon - the "Mediocre Recycled." These individuals are like zombies, shambling through the halls of venture-backed startups, sucking the life out of innovation.

What is the Mediocre Recycled? They're executives who have been recycled from one mediocre company to another, always playing it safe, never pushing boundaries. They're not truly innovators; they're just rehashers of tired ideas, clinging to outdated strategies that worked (or didn't) five or ten years ago.

Here's how you can spot them:

4. **They're allergic to risk-taking**: Any proposal that involves real experimentation or calculated bets will be met with skepticism, dismissed as too "ambitious."

These Mediocre Recycled executives infect entire organizations with their cautionary approach. They stifle innovation, prioritize short-term gains over long-term growth, and ultimately lead to stagnation.

To avoid these zombie executives, ask tough questions during interviews:

* Can you describe your most significant failure and what you learned from it?
* What was the last time you took a genuine risk on an unproven idea?
* How do you measure success beyond vanity metrics?

If their responses sound rehearsed or lack conviction, trust your instincts and keep looking. Your startup deserves better than a Mediocre Recycled executive siphoning off its potential energy.

**The Honest Truth About Co-Founder Equity**

Hey fellow founders,

I've been asked this question a thousand times at SaaStr events and conferences, but I still think it's worth addressing. 

How common are equal equity splits among co-founders?

Honestly, super rare.

In my experience (and based on conversations with hundreds of other successful startup founders), most co-founder teams end up with unequal splits. Sometimes significantly so.

Now before everyone starts freaking out, let me clarify:

Unequal splits don't mean one founder owns more than the others; they often reflect different levels of contribution, risk tolerance, or value added to the business from day one.

For example, if you have two co-founders where one brings a strong network and connections, while the other handles product development, their contributions may not be directly comparable - making an even split unfair to both parties.

Or what if one cofounder takes on significant financial risk by quitting their job to join the company full-time? Their role in the business changes dramatically after that point.

So how do you decide who gets what percentage? Here are some general guidelines:

1. **Contribution-based**: Allocate shares based on each member's unique strengths, skills, and effort.
2. **Risk-adjusted**: Consider the level of personal risk taken on by each founder, especially when leaving stable employment behind.
3. **Value-driven**: Weigh the actual impact each co-founder has made to the business.

It's essential to discuss these factors openly with your partner(s) early on, rather than letting them simmer into resentment later down the line

topic: Why Marketing Should Almost Never Report to Sales
prompt: Write a LinkedIn post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: Why Marketing Should Almost Never Report to Sales
text:
"Marketing and sales alignment is crucial, but here's the thing:

When marketing reports directly to sales, it creates an unhealthy dynamic. Suddenly, marketing becomes more focused on 'feeding the beast' (i.e., generating leads for sales) rather than building a sustainable brand strategy.

In this setup, marketing often compromises its vision and goals to appease sales. They might prioritize short-term gains over long-term growth, sacrificing their own credibility as thought leaders in the process.

As a result, you get:

* Marketing teams stuck in a cycle of constant lead generation, with little time or resources to develop meaningful content, build relationships, or drive real customer engagement.
* Brand messaging that's disjointed, confusing, or uninspired - because it's being dictated by sales needs rather than marketing expertise.
* A lack of innovation and creativity within marketing teams, as they're too busy churning out quick fixes to impress sales.

Now, I'm not saying there should be no collaboration between marketing and sales. Of course, there should! But when marketing reports directly to sales, it can create a toxic relationship where one team is constantly trying to meet the other's expectations at the expense of its own integrity.

So what's the alternative? 

* Make marketing report to product or CEO. This way, marketing has the freedom to focus on building a strong brand narrative, driving customer acquisition, and fostering deep relationships with your target audience.
* Establish clear KPIs and objectives that align with overall business goals, ensuring both marketing and sales are working towards the same outcomes.
* Encourage open communication and feedback loops

**The Great Debate: When to Raise, Even If You're Already Cash Flow Positive**

Hey fellow founders,

I get asked this question all the time: "Jason, we've got a ton of interest from VCs but are still profitable - should we raise?"

And my answer is always... it depends.

Here's what I mean:

If you're cash flow positive and growing like crazy, congratulations! That's an amazing position to be in. And yes, you can definitely consider raising money at this stage.

But here's why you might want to think twice before pulling that trigger:

1. **You don't need the capital**: If you're already generating more revenue than expenses, do you really need someone else's money to fuel your growth?
2. **VCs often come with strings attached**: Sure, they'll give you a fat check, but will they also take control of key decisions or insist on changes to your business model?

So when is it worth considering a raise even if you're profitable?

1. **To accelerate growth**: If you have a clear vision for how additional funding can help you scale faster and capture market share sooner, then go for it.
2. **To diversify risk**: If you're heavily reliant on one customer segment or geography, bringing in new investors could provide much-needed insurance against downturns.

Ultimately, whether or not to raise is up to each individual founder and their unique situation. My advice? Take your time, weigh the pros and cons carefully, and don't let FOMO (fear of missing out) cloud your judgment.

 **Equity Compensation**: As your company scales, equity compensation becomes more common. This aligns the VP's interests with those of shareholders, ensuring they're invested in long-term success rather than just short-term gains.

**The Great Enterprise SaaS Conundrum**

Hey fellow founders and CEOs,

I've been asked this question many times before, but it's still one that keeps me up at night. When you're closing deals worth hundreds of thousands of dollars (or more), what's the typical enterprise SaaS cancellation policy?

And should your contract even have a fine for cancelling early?

**Here are some general guidelines I'd recommend:**

1. **Notice period:** Typically 30-60 days' notice is standard. This gives both parties time to wrap things up.
2. **Termination fees:** These can range from 10% to 50% of the annual contract value (ACV). Yes, you read that right - 50%! But don't be afraid to negotiate these down based on your specific deal terms.
3. **No-fault termination clauses:** Make sure your contracts include language allowing either party to terminate without penalty if there's a material breach or insolvency.

Now, about those fines...

**Should your contract have a fine?**

In my opinion, no. Fines create unnecessary tension and can lead to disputes when they're applied unfairly. Instead, focus on building strong relationships with your customers and delivering exceptional value. If they want out, work together to find an amicable solution.

That being said... 

If you do decide to include a fine, make sure it's:

* Reasonable (e.g., tied to actual costs incurred)
* Clearly communicated upfront
* Not so high that it becomes a deterrent to new business

Ultimately, every situation is unique

* According to the American Bar Association, the average cost per hour for a litigator is over $500.

So what can you do instead?

* Focus on building relationships and trust with your partners, investors, and customers.
* Establish clear communication channels and expectations upfront.
* Know when to fold 'em (i.e., know when to walk away).

It may seem counterintuitive, but sometimes the smartest move is to concede defeat early on. Not because you're admitting fault, but because you value your sanity, your wallet, and your future success

"Hey fellow founders and entrepreneurs,

I've been asked this question many times, but never got around to answering it explicitly. So here's my take:

**Do companies prefer stock over cash when they acquire startups?**

Short answer: **yes**, increasingly so.

Longer answer: In today's startup landscape, we're seeing more acquirers opting for stock rather than cash as part of their M&A strategy. Why?

1. **Tax implications**: Allowing sellers to receive equity reduces tax liabilities on gains from the sale.
2. **Risk-sharing**: By giving up some of the upside through dilution, buyers can share risk with the seller.
3. **Retain talent**: If an acquisition target has key employees who are also shareholders, offering them stock or options can help retain top talent.
4. **Future growth potential**: As valuations continue to rise, receiving stock in lieu of cash provides sellers with exposure to future appreciation.
5. **Alignment**: Buyers want to align incentives between themselves and the acquired team; issuing shares achieves that alignment.

That being said, there are still scenarios where all-cash deals make sense – like when you have a high-growth business with limited runway or need immediate liquidity.

As always, every situation is unique, and what works for one company may not work for another.

What are your thoughts on stock vs. cash acquisitions? Share your experiences and insights!

So here's my take:

**Don't believe them (initially)**. Just because someone says they don't invest in your space doesn't mean it's true. Often, it means one of two things:

1. **They're not interested in talking to you**: Maybe their team is too busy or maybe they just aren't the right fit for your company.
2. **They're trying to deflect interest**: Sometimes, VCs will say they don't invest in a particular area just to avoid getting inundated with pitches from companies that might be interesting, but outside their 'wheelhouse'.

**Do some digging**: Before giving up on a potential investor, do some research and see if there have been any notable investments in your space recently. If so, ask yourself:
- Has this VC invested in similar spaces before?
- Are there any obvious reasons why they wouldn't invest in your specific area?

**Look beyond the initial response**: It's easy to get discouraged by an initial "no", but don't let it stop you. Keep building relationships with other investors and eventually, you'll find the ones who align best with your vision.

And remember, even the most successful startups started somewhere - often in niches where others said no.

How have you handled situations like these in your own fundraising journey? Share your experiences and insights below!

Happy funding

2. **Triggering the Reserve**: When you hit specific milestones or experience certain events (e.g., rapid growth, increased competition), you can trigger the reserve. This notifies the VC firm that you require additional funds.
3. **Additional Capital**: The VC firm then releases the reserved amount, providing you with the necessary resources to address emerging opportunities or challenges.

Benefits of reserve funding:

- Reduced reliance on new investors and associated dilution
- More flexible access to capital when needed
- Strengthened relationships with existing VCs

However, be aware that reserve funding often comes with conditions and requirements. These may include:
- Meeting specific performance targets
- Implementing strategic initiatives
- Reporting regular updates to the VC firm

To effectively utilize reserve funding, focus on building strong relationships with your VCs and maintaining transparent communication throughout your journey.

text:
**Don't Fear Business Process Change. It's (Usually) a Good Thing**

Ladies and gentlemen, today I want to talk about something that might seem scary at first, but trust me, it's not as terrifying as you think – business process change.

As founders and CEOs, we're always looking for ways to grow our companies faster, more efficiently, and with better results. And let's be honest, sometimes those changes can feel like they're going to disrupt everything we've worked so hard to build.

But here's the thing: business process change is not inherently bad. In fact, it's usually a good thing. Think about it this way: when was the last time you took on a new challenge or implemented a new system that didn't require some level of adjustment? Wasn't there an initial learning curve? Didn't things get a little messy before they got smoother?

That's exactly what happens during business process change. We're forced to confront areas where we can improve, streamline operations, reduce waste, and increase efficiency. It's a natural part of growth, and if we don't embrace it, we risk stagnation and complacency.

Now, I know what you're thinking: "Jason, isn't changing processes just a recipe for disaster?" Well, yes and no. If done poorly, any major change can lead to chaos, lost productivity, and frustration among employees. But if executed well, with careful planning, clear communication, and a willingness to adapt, the benefits far outweigh the costs.

So how do you make sure your business process change doesn't become a nightmare? Here are three key takeaways:

First, **start small**. You don't need to overhaul every aspect of your company at once. Pick one area where you see room for improvement and focus on making incremental changes. This will allow you to test the waters without overwhelming yourself or your team.

Second, **communicate clearly**. When introducing change, people need context, explanation, and reassurance. Be transparent about why you're making these changes and how they'll benefit everyone involved. Encourage feedback and involve stakeholders throughout the process.

Third, **measure and adjust**. After implementing your changes, keep track of metrics that matter most to your business. Are sales up? Is customer satisfaction higher? Did employee morale improve? Use data to refine your approach and make adjustments as needed.

In conclusion, business process change should be viewed as an opportunity rather than a threat. By embracing change and following these simple principles, you'll position your company for long-term success, increased agility, and ultimately, explosive growth.

So go ahead, be bold, and start experimenting with new processes. Your competitors won't wait for you to catch up!

Thank you!

text:
**Title:** Be Honest If Growth Has Slowed. Is Your Product Still Magical? It Probably... Used To Be.

**Hello, everyone!**

I'm thrilled to be here today talking about one of my favorite topics - growth hacking. As many of you know, I've been fortunate enough to have had some amazing successes with my own companies, like EchoSign and Nimble. But let's get real for a second. Not every company is going to scale as quickly or as easily as we might hope.

And that's okay. That's actually more than okay. Because when growth starts slowing down, it forces us to confront something really important: are our products still magical?

Now, I want to define what "magical" means to me. A product is magical when it solves a problem so well that users can't imagine living without it. When they're willing to pay top dollar for it because it makes their lives better in some fundamental way. And most importantly, when its value proposition continues to grow even after the initial excitement wears off.

But here's the thing: once your product has solved a basic need, getting people to continue using it becomes much harder. You see, humans have this weird psychological phenomenon called "the law of diminishing returns." In short, things stop making us happy at a certain point, no matter how great they were initially.

So, if growth has slowed down, ask yourself: did our product ever truly solve a deeply felt pain point? Or was it just a novelty at first, but now feels repetitive or boring to use?

Let me give you an example from my past experience with EchoSign (which later became DocuSign). Initially, our e-signature solution was revolutionary. People loved signing documents digitally instead of printing them out and faxing them around. We grew fast, really fast. But over time, people started to take online signatures for granted. They assumed all software would work similarly. Our innovation wasn't unique anymore; it was expected.

Here's another question to consider: do customers still rave about our product? Do they tell others about how life-changing it is? Or does it feel like a necessary evil, something they use only because someone told them too?

If you find that your product isn't sparking joy or enthusiasm like it used to, then maybe it's not magical anymore. Maybe it's time to re-examine what we mean by 'growth' and whether there are other metrics worth measuring.

Instead of focusing solely on revenue or user acquisition costs, perhaps we should prioritize product stickiness, customer retention rates, or Net Promoter Scores. These metrics often reveal deeper issues within our business models.

As entrepreneurs, we must learn to accept that growth will slow down eventually. The key is recognizing why it happened in the first place. Was it due to saturation in the market? Did competitors catch up? Or did we simply become complacent?

By acknowledging these challenges head-on and adjusting our strategies accordingly, we increase our chances of creating truly magical experiences – ones where customers keep coming back for more, and refer friends with glee.

In conclusion, don't be afraid to admit if growth has slowed. Don't pretend everything's fine when, deep down, you suspect otherwise. Ask yourself honestly: is my product still magical? Chances are, it probably... used to be. Let's face reality together and make adjustments before it's too late!

Thank you for listening, folks!

**Philip Rathle**: Another significant hurdle we faced was data management. As customer base grew, so did their data volumes. To resolve this, we implemented advanced indexing techniques and caching mechanisms, which significantly enhanced query performance and ensured seamless user experiences even under heavy loads.

**Jason Lemkin**: Those are exactly the kinds of technical hurdles you need to overcome to reach $100 million ARR. What advice would you give entrepreneurs facing similar product development and scalability issues?

Identify areas where your product might cause friction or create pain points early on and tackle these problems before they become major obstacles. Surround yourself with experts who can guide you through complex decisions, whether it's hiring specialized talent or engaging outside consultants.

**Philip Rathle**: The pleasure is mine, Jason. Scaling is never straightforward, but knowing where potential pitfalls lie can make all the difference between achieving and falling short of that coveted $100 million ARR goal.

**Jason Lemkin**: Absolutely right. If you're struggling with similar challenges, remember that every successful entrepreneur faces similar struggles. topic: Thinking of Being a VP at a Venture-Backed Startup? Think Twice
prompt: Write a talk in the style of Jason Lemkin about: Thinking of Being a VP at a Venture-Backed Startup? Think Twice
text:
**Jason Lemkin here, and today I want to share with you something that I wish someone had told me when I was just starting out.**

As many of you know, my career has been pretty unconventional – from early-stage sales leader to successful founder, investor, and now CEO coach. And through it all, I've seen a lot of talented people take on roles that they're not quite ready for.

Specifically, I'm talking about VPs at venture-backed startups.

Now, being a VP can be an incredible experience – the responsibility, the challenge, the opportunity to make real impact. But let's get one thing straight: being a VP is not for everyone. In fact, if you think about becoming a VP without carefully considering your own strengths, weaknesses, and goals... well, you might find yourself in over your head.

So what are some things to consider before taking on this role?

First, **you need to have a deep understanding of the business**, inside and out. This isn't just about knowing how to sell or market; it's about having a comprehensive grasp of finance, operations, product development – everything that goes into making a startup succeed.

Second, **you need to be able to handle ambiguity**. As a VP, you'll be working closely with the CEO and other executives to drive strategy and decision-making. That means navigating uncertain situations, communicating effectively under pressure, and staying focused even when there aren't clear answers.

Third, **you need to be willing to roll up your sleeves**. At most startups, especially those backed by venture capital, everyone wears multiple hats. You may need to trade off responsibilities between departments or help lead cross-functional projects. It takes humility, flexibility, and a willingness to learn new skills.

Fourth, **you need to prioritize relationships**. Building trust with colleagues, investors, customers – these are essential components of success as a VP. Fostering strong networks will serve you well both personally and professionally.

Lastly, **consider whether this aligns with your long-term goals**. While being a VP can provide immense personal growth opportunities, it also requires significant time commitment. Are you prepared to put in the hours required to excel in this role, while potentially sacrificing aspects of your personal life?

If you still feel like becoming a VP after thinking through these considerations, then great! The journey ahead will undoubtedly be challenging but rewarding.

However, if you're unsure or hesitant, don't worry. There are plenty of alternative paths where you can grow and contribute meaningfully within a company without feeling overwhelmed or stuck. Consider more junior leadership positions, team leads, or special projects – each offers valuable learning experiences without the same level of responsibility.

In conclusion, being a VP at a venture-backed startup is not for the faint of heart. Before embarking on this path, make sure you understand its demands, challenges, and rewards. Ask yourself hard questions, seek guidance from mentors, and weigh your priorities against the potential benefits. If you do decide to pursue this role, remember that every step forward requires courage, resilience, and adaptability.

topic: 8 Ideas to Help Make Sure Your Team … Stays
prompt: Write a talk in the style of Jason Lemkin about: 8 Ideas to Help Make Sure Your Team … Stays
text:
**Hello, everyone! I'm thrilled to be here today talking about one of my favorite topics - building and retaining top-notch teams. As many of you know, at SaaStr we've seen thousands of companies grow from zero to millions in revenue, but it's not just about scaling the business - it's also about keeping your A-players on board. So let's dive into eight ideas that can help ensure your team stays with you for the long haul.**

1. **Give Them Autonomy**: One thing I love about working with entrepreneurs is their willingness to take risks. And when it comes to employee retention, giving them autonomy is key. Give your team members the freedom to make decisions without needing approval from higher-ups every step of the way.

At EchoSign (which was later acquired by Airtable), we had an open-door policy where anyone could come up with new features or products as long as they presented them to our CEO. This encouraged innovation, creativity, and ownership among employees. The result? Some amazing products were born out of this process!

2. **Create Meaningful Work**: When people join your company, they want to feel like what they're doing matters. It's essential to connect their individual goals with those of the organization. In other words, give them something bigger than themselves to strive for.

Our early success at Palantir was due in large part because we tackled complex problems that made a real difference in society. Employees knew they were contributing to something meaningful. Today, many companies are starting to prioritize social responsibility and sustainability initiatives within their organizations.

3. **Build Strong Relationships**: Building relationships between colleagues is crucial for creating a positive work environment. Encourage teamwork, collaboration, and open communication.

When I joined Echosign back in the day, we were still pretty small. But our founder, Dave LaGesse, would often have regular 'town hall' meetings where everyone could share updates and ask questions. Those sessions helped build camaraderie and fostered trust across departments.

4. **Foster Growth Opportunities**: Every person wants to learn and develop professionally. Create opportunities for growth through training programs, mentorship, and clear career paths.

One reason I think we retained so much talent during my time at EchoSign was because we invested heavily in professional development. We even offered a stipend for courses or certifications that aligned with each role's requirements.

5. **Recognize & Reward Performance**: Show your team how much you appreciate their hard work by recognizing outstanding performance. This doesn't necessarily mean bonuses; sometimes simple gestures go further.

We used to have quarterly celebrations called "EchoAwards" which honored individuals who went above and beyond in terms of customer satisfaction ratings or sales numbers. These little perks reminded folks why all their efforts mattered!

6. **Offer Flexible Work Arrangements**: With remote work becoming more common these days, flexibility has become essential for attracting and retaining top talent.

In fact, studies show that nearly half of workers report being more productive while working remotely compared to office settings. At SaaStr, we encourage flexible schedules whenever possible – knowing that people need balance between personal life and job responsibilities.

7. **Celebrate Milestones & Successes**: Celebrate milestones achieved both individually and collectively. Acknowledge progress toward larger organizational objectives too.

During big launches or product releases at EchoSign, we'd throw parties and invite friends and family. That sense of community created lasting memories for employees.

8. **Communicate Clearly & Honestly**: Lastly, communicate openly with your team. Be transparent regarding expectations, challenges ahead, and future plans. If things aren't going well, own up to mistakes rather than sweeping them under the rug.

From my experience running multiple startups, honesty builds trust faster than anything else ever will. Don't underestimate its power.

So there

topic: Raising Money After a Rough Patch? At Least Put Up 3 Good Months in a Row
prompt: Write a talk in the style of Jason Lemkin about: Raising Money After a Rough Patch? At Least Put Up 3 Good Months in a Row
text:
**Raising Money After a Rough Patch**

Good morning everyone, and thank you for having me here today. As many of you know, I've been through my fair share of ups and downs as an entrepreneur. And let's be real – every startup is going to hit some rough patches along the way.

But what happens when those rough patches turn into months, or even quarters, of struggle? How do you bounce back from that kind of setback? Today, I want to talk about raising money after a tough period, and how you can put yourself on track to raise again by showing consistent growth over at least three good months in a row.

Now, before we dive in, I want to acknowledge that this isn't easy advice. In fact, it's often counterintuitive to think about fundraising during a down time. But trust me, if you're willing to put in the hard work upfront, you'll set your company up for long-term success – and make investors more likely to take notice.

So, why are three good months so important?

Firstly, they give you credibility with potential investors. Think about it – most VCs will tell you that they love companies with momentum. When you show consistent growth month-over-month, it sends a clear signal that your business model is working, and that you have a team capable of executing on it.

Secondly, three good months provide a baseline for future projections. Investors want to see that you have a proven track record of delivering results, which makes them feel more confident in their investment decision.

And finally, achieving consistency over multiple months shows resilience. It demonstrates that your business has weathered any initial hiccups, and is now built to last.

Now, I know what you might be thinking – "Jason, this all sounds great in theory, but what about my specific situation?" Maybe you had one bad quarter due to unforeseen circumstances, like supply chain disruptions or economic downturns. Or maybe your product just didn't resonate with customers initially.

The point is, there's no such thing as a perfect startup. Every company faces challenges, and sometimes those challenges lead to setbacks. But what matters is how quickly you adapt, learn from those mistakes, and get back on track.

Here's the key takeaway:

You don't need a string of consecutive wins to prove your worth to investors. What you need is a solid foundation of consistent performance over several months. This gives investors confidence that you have a viable business strategy, a talented team behind it, and a proven ability to execute.

In practice, this looks different for each company. For some startups, it means focusing on customer acquisition costs (CAC) and revenue growth metrics. Others may prioritize retention rates or operational efficiency.

For our SaaStr community, I recommend tracking these core metrics:

1. Customer Acquisition Costs (CAC)
2. Revenue Growth Rate (YoY or QoQ)
3. Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)
4. Net Retention Rate (NRR)

These KPIs will help you pinpoint areas where you need improvement, and demonstrate progress over time.

Lastly, remember that fundraising is not just about getting cash; it's also about building relationships. Network with other entrepreneurs who have gone through similar experiences. Attend conferences, join online forums, and connect with people who understand your pain points.

When you finally sit down with investors, be prepared to explain the steps you took to recover from your rough patch. Share lessons learned, new strategies implemented, and tangible improvements made. Show them that you've done the hard work required to emerge stronger than ever.

topic: 5 Interesting Learnings from Toast at $500m in ARR, and a $3B Total Run Rate
prompt: Write a talk in the style of Jason Lemkin about: 5 Interesting Learnings from Toast at $500m in ARR, and a $3B Total Run Rate
text:
**Jason Lemkin Style Talk**

Good morning everyone. Today I want to dive into some really interesting learnings from one of my favorite companies, Toast. If you're not familiar with them, they're a restaurant management platform that has grown incredibly fast over the last few years.

As an investor in growth-stage SaaS companies, I've had the chance to dig deep into their story and what's driving their success. And today, I'm excited to share five key takeaways that can be applied to any high-growth startup like yours.

So let's get started!

**Learning #1: Focus on the Middle Market**

Toast has been able to dominate the middle market - think restaurants with 10-50 locations - by providing a more comprehensive solution than their competitors. They offer everything from online ordering and delivery integration to inventory management and payroll processing.

This focus on the middle market has allowed them to scale much faster than other players who are trying to tackle smaller or larger restaurants. By targeting this sweet spot, Toast has been able to achieve massive traction and build a loyal customer base.

**Learning #2: It's Not Just About Software; It's About Services**

While Toast is primarily a software company, they understand that delivering value requires more than just code. Their services team provides support, training, and even consulting services to help restaurants implement and optimize their system.

By offering these additional services, Toast has created a stickier relationship with its customers and increased retention rates. This approach also allows them to upsell and cross-sell new features and solutions, further accelerating revenue growth.

**Learning #3: Go Deep Before You Go Wide**

When Toast was still relatively small, they focused on building strong relationships with a limited number of large customers rather than spreading themselves too thin across many smaller ones. This allowed them to refine their product and deliver exceptional results for those early adopters.

Once they'd perfected their solution, they expanded to the wider market, leveraging their existing network effects to drive adoption even further. This "go deep" strategy helped Toast establish itself as a leader in the industry before expanding its reach.

**Learning #4: Don't Be Afraid to Invest Heavily in Customer Success**

At $500 million in ARR, Toast has invested heavily in building out its customer success organization. This includes dedicated account managers, implementation specialists, and analytics teams working closely together to ensure every customer gets the most out of their investment.

By prioritizing customer success, Toast has reduced churn and improved satisfaction rates while simultaneously increasing average deal size through upsells and cross-sells. As your business scales, don't underestimate the importance of investing in people who truly care about making your customers successful.

**Learning #5: Data-Driven Decision Making Is Key**

Finally, Toast relies heavily on data-driven decision-making throughout all levels of the organization. From analyzing customer behavior and user engagement to optimizing pricing and sales strategies, their use of data informs nearly every major choice.

As your own business grows, it becomes increasingly difficult to keep track of multiple variables without automation. Implementing robust data tools will enable you to make informed decisions quickly and adapt rapidly to changing circumstances.

In conclusion, Toast's remarkable journey offers valuable lessons for any high-growth startup looking to replicate their success. Remember to:

* Target the right segment of the market where you can create significant impact.
* Offer both products and services to deepen customer relationships.
* Prioritize going deep before expanding wide.
* Make substantial investments in customer success to reduce churn and increase ARPU.
* Use data to inform critical decisions that propel your business forward.

Thanks for joining me today! Do you have any questions about Toast or how to apply these insights to your own business? Let's discuss!

I'm Jason Lemkin, and as an entrepreneur who's been through it all – from early struggles to massive success with EchoSign (now DocuSign) and later at SaaStr, I'll share my insights on what sets apart those companies that reach critical mass from those that don't.**

You see, we're not just talking about any old growth here; we're discussing **initial traction**, where your business transforms into something real, scalable, and potentially game-changing.

So, let me ask you this: Are you tired of wondering whether your hard work will pay off? Do you want to stop guessing when it comes to your company's potential?

Well, wonder no more!

In my experience, there are several key indicators of initial traction in SaaS:

1. **Consistent Revenue Growth**: This one might seem obvious, but trust me, it's crucial. Your revenue should be growing month-over-month without much effort or additional investment.

To give you some perspective, our team at EchoSign saw consistent revenue growth for over two years before reaching $10 million ARR. And once we reached that milestone, we were unstoppable.

2. **Customer Acquisition Costs Decrease Over Time**: If your CAC is consistently decreasing, it means you're getting better at acquiring customers efficiently.

Think of it like building a flywheel: every new customer acquired reduces marketing spend per acquisition because you can leverage word-of-mouth, referrals, and existing relationships.

At SaaStr, we've seen numerous companies achieve this sweet spot by perfecting their sales funnels and scaling their go-to-market strategies effectively.

3. **Net Promoter Score Improves**: A high NPS indicates happy customers, which leads to retention, positive word-of-mouth, and ultimately, increased revenue.

For example, if your average customer satisfaction rating goes up significantly after implementing changes based on user feedback, it's likely you've reached a level of maturity in your product development process.

4. **Organizational Structure Changes**: As you scale, so does your org chart. Expect roles to shift toward support functions like sales ops, customer success teams, and even dedicated account management positions.

We experienced rapid growth at EchoSign, which necessitated shifting our focus from being primarily engineers to creating an entire infrastructure around customer support, ensuring seamless delivery of our software solution.

5. **Your Team’s Mindset Shifts**: They start believing they have a winning formula and begin looking ahead rather than focusing solely on survival.

As entrepreneurs, you must recognize these signs within yourselves first, then watch them manifest throughout the rest of the organization.

topic: An Underused Strategy: Truly High Value Drip Marketing to Prospects
prompt: Write a talk in the style of Jason Lemkin about: An Underused Strategy: Truly High Value Drip Marketing to Prospects
text:
**Jason Lemkin Style Talk**

Ladies and gentlemen, today I want to talk about something that I believe is an underutilized strategy for SaaS companies looking to grow their sales pipeline. It's not about throwing more money at advertising or hiring more sales reps. No, it's actually quite simple yet powerful.

I'm talking about high-value drip marketing to prospects.

Now, you might be thinking, "Drip marketing? Isn't that just sending a bunch of emails to people who haven't even shown any interest?" Well, no. Not when done correctly. When we say high-value drip marketing, we're talking about creating a carefully crafted series of messages designed to educate and engage our target audience over time.

The goal here isn't to spam them with irrelevant content or try to close deals too quickly. No, the goal is to build trust, establish authority, and create value in your prospect's life before ever asking for anything in return.

So how do we do this?

First, identify the pain points and interests of your ideal customer. What keeps them up at night? What are they trying to solve? Use this information to craft relevant and valuable content that speaks directly to those needs.

Next, use automation tools like Mailchimp, Hubspot, or Pardot to set up a sequence of email campaigns that deliver this content over time. Each message should be strategically placed to address a specific aspect of the buyer's journey.

For example:

1. Message #1: Introduction to your company and its mission.
2. Message #2: Explaining a key challenge facing your industry (and how you can help).
3. Message #3: Showcasing success stories from similar customers.
4. Message #4: Offering actionable tips or resources on solving common problems.
5. And so on...

Here's the thing: these messages shouldn't feel forced or sales-y. They should genuinely add value to the prospect's day-to-day life. That means no hard sells, no pushy language, and definitely no clickbait headlines.

By doing this, you're building credibility, establishing thought leadership, and slowly but surely educating your prospect on why your solution is worth considering.

And here's where most people screw it up:

They get impatient. They think, "Okay, great, I've got my drip campaign going out. Now let's just wait for leads to pour in." But that's not how it works.

High-value drip marketing takes time – weeks, months, sometimes even years – to bear fruit. You need to commit to the process, refine your messaging based on feedback and data analysis, and continually optimize for better results.

But if you stick with it, the rewards can be significant. For one, you'll see increased conversion rates as prospects become increasingly engaged and educated throughout the buying process. Second, you'll reduce the number of unqualified leads entering your funnel because they'll have already demonstrated a willingness to learn from your brand.

Lastly, by providing genuine value upfront, you're setting yourself up for long-term relationships rather than short-sighted transactions. Think about it: which would you rather have – someone who bought from you once or someone who will continue to purchase from you repeatedly over the next decade?

That's what truly high-value drip marketing is all about. So don't waste another dollar on ineffective lead gen tactics. Invest in the power of education, engagement, and relationship-building through high-quality drip marketing.

Let me leave you with one final question: Are you ready to put the effort into creating real value for your potential customers? If so, then join me in embracing this often-overlooked strategy for driving sustainable growth in your business. Thank you!

topic: Why Every B2B Software Company is About to Become a Backend Service. You Need To Get Ahead Of It.
prompt: Write a talk in the style of Jason Lemkin about: Why Every B2B Software Company is About to Become a Backend Service. You Need To Get Ahead Of It.
text:
**Title:** The Shift is Coming: Why Every B2B Software Company Needs to Think Like a Backend Service

**Hello everyone,**

I'm excited to share with you today why I believe every B2B software company will soon become a backend service by default. And let me tell you, this shift has massive implications for how we build and operate our businesses.

As many of you know, I've spent my fair share of time building, scaling, and advising SaaS companies over the years. But what's happening now is a fundamental transformation that requires us all to rethink our business models, product strategies, and operational approaches.

So, here are the reasons why I firmly believe that every B2B software company needs to think like a backend service:

1. **API Economy**: With the rise of API-first development, we're witnessing an explosion of APIs being exposed as products themselves. This means that traditional SaaS companies can no longer rely solely on their UI/UX to drive value. Instead, they need to focus on providing high-quality, scalable, and secure backends that power multiple applications.

2. **Decoupling User Interfaces**: As more users interact with your platform through various devices, channels, or third-party integrations, decoupling user interfaces from core functionality becomes essential. By exposing APIs and providing a robust backend, you ensure seamless experiences across different touchpoints.

3. **Monetization Strategies**: In the past, SaaS companies focused primarily on subscription-based revenue streams. However, with the growth of open-source alternatives and freemium offerings, it's becoming increasingly difficult to maintain premium pricing. By offering APIs and services à la carte, you can create new revenue opportunities and adapt to changing market dynamics.

4. **Competitive Advantage**: Those who transition early will have a significant head start in terms of developing expertise in backend architecture, security, and scalability. They'll also be better positioned to capitalize on emerging trends such as serverless computing, edge computing, and real-time analytics.

5. **Partnerships and Ecosystems**: A strong backend infrastructure enables easier integration with other solutions, fostering partnerships and ecosystems around your platform. This not only expands your reach but also creates new revenue streams through data exchange, co-marketing initiatives, or joint R&D efforts.

Now, I want to emphasize that becoming a backend service doesn't mean abandoning your existing customers or neglecting your front-end experience. Rather, it involves recognizing that your core strength lies in delivering reliable, efficient, and flexible backends that underpin everything else.

To get ahead of this shift, consider these key takeaways:

- **Replatform and modernize**: Invest in cloud-native architectures, containerization, and DevOps practices to ensure your backbone is ready for the demands of tomorrow.
- **API-first design**: Prioritize designing APIs that are intuitive, well-documented, and easy to consume, allowing developers to integrate your services seamlessly into their workflows.
- **Scalable engineering**: Develop a culture of experimentation and continuous improvement, always seeking ways to optimize performance, reliability, and efficiency within your backend operations.
- **Platform thinking**: View your company as a platform provider rather than just a product vendor. Focus on creating a rich ecosystem where partners, developers, and end-users can contribute, innovate, and grow together.

In conclusion, embracing the role of a backend service will require bold strategic decisions, investments in talent and technology, and a willingness to disrupt established norms. But trust me when I say that those who lead this charge will reap enormous rewards – both financially and competitively.

It's time to get ahead of the curve. Your future depends on it.

Thank you!

It's not just about being innovative; it's not just about having a great idea. It's about understanding what drives real disruption. And often, entrepreneurs get this wrong. They confuse room at the bottom with disruption.

So, let me define these two terms for you:

*   **Room at the bottom**: This is when you're targeting customers who are already using an existing product but need more affordable options.
*   **Disruption**: This is when you create new markets, new customer segments, or new business models that didn't exist before.

Now, here's why many founders mistakenly think they're disrupting their industry when all they're really doing is creating a cheaper version of someone else's product.

They see other companies making money in the market and assume there must be untapped demand. So, they launch their own products, cutting prices to win over those customers. Sounds like a good strategy? Not quite.

When you focus solely on price competition, you'll never disrupt anything. You might capture some market share, sure, but you won't change the game. The incumbent players will always find ways to keep up with your pricing, even if it means sacrificing profit margins.

Here's another example. Suppose you start a new e-commerce platform focused on budget-friendly fashion. You might gain traction initially by offering cheap clothing options, but eventually, established brands will adapt to compete with you on price. Your growth will stall because you haven't created any lasting impact on the industry.

To truly disrupt, you need to identify areas where existing solutions fall short or don't cater to emerging needs. Think of Airbnb, Uber, or Slack - these companies didn't merely offer cheaper alternatives to hotels, taxis, or email; they redefined how people live, travel, and work together.

If you genuinely aspire to revolutionize your industry, ask yourself questions like:

1.  Are we solving problems no one else has tackled?
2.  Are our customers willing to pay a premium for unique value propositions?
3.  Can we redefine the norms around how businesses operate?

In conclusion, while pursuing room at the bottom may bring temporary gains, true disruption requires vision, innovation, and courage. If you settle for simply competing on price, you risk getting left behind as others innovate and disrupt the space around you.

Thanks for listening!

**How Many Sales Reps Do You Really Need to Hit Your Plan for the Year?**

Hello, everyone. Today we're going to tackle one of my favorite topics - sales rep productivity and hiring strategies.

You know how it goes - you've got your annual plan set, with all those revenue targets and growth projections that you need to meet or exceed. And then there's this nagging question: "How many sales reps do I really need to make this happen?"

I used to think that the answer was straightforward - just divide your total target by each individual rep's quota, right? But over the years, through countless conversations with founders and CEOs like yourselves, I've come to realize that it's not quite that simple.

In fact, if you ask most companies how many sales reps they have on staff, they'll tell you somewhere around half what they actually need to hit their plan. That's because when you first hire someone new, they're essentially at zero velocity - no pipeline, no momentum, no deals closed yet.

So let me give you some updated math:

1. **Your actual headcount**: Let's say your company has an ambitious goal of $10 million ARR this year.
2. **Average sales cycle length**: This is the time between when a prospect becomes aware of your product and when they close as a customer. It can vary widely depending on your business model and industry, but a good rule of thumb is 6-12 months.
3. **Monthly run rate**: Take your total target ($10 million) and divide it by 12 months to get a monthly run rate. In our case, that would be $833,333 per month.

Now here comes the important part:

To calculate the minimum number of sales reps needed to hit your plan, take your monthly run rate and multiply it by the average sales cycle length divided by three.

Sounds weird, I know, but bear with me.

For example:
$833,333 / month x 9-month sales cycle = $7,444,999 
Then divide the above result by $250,000 
The final result will be approximately 30 sales reps 

But wait, there's more! We still haven't accounted for ramp-up time, which means that even after you onboard a new rep, it takes them several months to reach full speed.

Assuming a moderate ramp-up period of 4-5 months, where your new rep reaches only 25% of their quota, we should add another 50% to account for this lag.

**That's why I recommend having roughly twice as many sales reps as you initially think you need to hit your plan.**

Of course, every company is unique, and these numbers are merely guidelines. However, the next time you find yourself wondering whether to hire another rep, remember: it might seem expensive upfront, but not doing so could lead to missing your goals entirely.

By understanding the true dynamics of sales team productivity and planning ahead, you can avoid common pitfalls like under-resourcing and ensure you stay on track to meet or exceed your growth objectives.

Thanks for joining me today. If you want to learn more about scaling sales teams efficiently, feel free to DM me anytime. Happy selling!

text:
**The Pitch Conference, San Francisco**

Ladies and gentlemen, founders, and fellow entrepreneurs, I'm Jason Lemkin here today to give you some hard truths about your VC relationships. As an investor myself and having been through multiple funding rounds with various startups, I've seen firsthand what it takes to succeed – or fail.

You're probably sitting there thinking, "Jason, we just raised $10 million, our growth is accelerating, and our product is killing it." But let me tell you something that might make your stomach drop: your VCs may be giving up on you right now.

Now before I dive into this, let's set the context. Venture capital is a high-risk business, and investors are constantly weighing their bets. They invest in maybe five to seven companies per year out of hundreds they review. When those investments don't pan out as expected, VCs get anxious. And when anxiety sets in, they start looking for reasons to exit or re-evaluate their commitment.

Here are a few signs that your VCs might be losing faith:

1. **Less frequent check-ins**: If you notice fewer meetings or less communication from your investors, that could be a sign they're disengaging.
2. **Changes in investment thesis**: If your VCs suddenly change their focus or pivot away from your company, it might indicate they no longer see value in your vision.
3. **Reduced support for key initiatives**: When investors start pulling back on resources, it can signal they're not confident in your ability to execute.

But here's the thing: these changes shouldn't stop you from pushing forward. In fact, they should fuel your determination even more. Think about it: if your VCs have doubts, it means there's still room for improvement, and that's exactly where innovation happens.

So how do you respond? First, acknowledge the situation. Have open conversations with your investors to understand their concerns. Listen actively, but also don't be afraid to push back and explain why you believe in your vision.

Second, refocus on execution. Prove your doubters wrong by delivering results. This isn't about winning arguments; it's about demonstrating traction.

Third, diversify your investor base. While it's great to have strong partnerships, relying too heavily on one or two investors can create dependency issues. Consider expanding your network and exploring alternative sources of funding.

Lastly, remember that VCs come and go. The best investors will ride the waves with you, while others will bail at the first sign of turbulence. Focus on building a loyal community around your startup, and prioritize relationships with partners who genuinely care about your success.

In conclusion, your VCs may be giving up on you right now, but don't let that discourage you. Use this moment as an opportunity to prove them wrong, refine your strategy, and build a stronger foundation for long-term success.

Remember, every successful entrepreneur has faced adversity along the way. Steve Jobs was fired from Apple twice, Walt Disney went bankrupt several times, and Henry Ford failed numerous experiments before perfecting his assembly line. So don't let the doubts of others define your path.

Keep pushing forward, stay true to your vision, and most importantly, never lose sight of why you started this journey in the first place. Thank you!

**Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to today's discussion on 'prosumer' vibe coding. I'm Jason Lemkin, and as you know, I've spent years building successful SaaS companies from scratch. Now, let's dive into some hard truths that no one likes to discuss when it comes to creating real-world B2B apps with this unique coding approach.**

---

### **The Unspoken Truths Behind Prosumer Vibes In Code**

As founders, we often get caught up in chasing the latest tech trends or trying to build something entirely new and revolutionary. However, if your goal is to create a sustainable, profitable B2B app that solves actual problems for businesses, there are certain principles you need to understand – and I'm here to share them.

Let's break down eight essential things no one tells you about prosumer vibes in code:

#### **1. Forget About "Sexy" Tech Stacks For A Second**

We all love talking about React, Angular, or GraphQL because they sound impressive on LinkedIn posts. But what matters most isn't which technology you use; it's how well it integrates, performs under pressure, and provides value to your customers. When it comes to B2B applications, stability and reliability should be your top priorities over cutting-edge features.

#### **2. Your Users Will Use It Wrong**

In theory, every user will read the manual, follow best practices, and never encounter any issues. Reality checks in quickly, though. They'll click buttons out of sequence, forget passwords, or just plain old mess with settings. Anticipate these scenarios by incorporating robust error handling, clear UI feedback, and accessible support resources.

#### **3. Integration Is Where The Magic Happens (Or Breaks)**

One thing everyone loves discussing is the perfect API architecture, but very few people focus on integration complexity. Think about all those external services you're integrating: payment gateways, CRM systems, third-party APIs... The list goes on. Not only do you have to handle different response formats, errors, and latency, but also ensure seamless handovers between services. Plan carefully to avoid costly rework later on.

#### **4. Security Isn’t An Afterthought – It’s Always First**

I see so many teams that prioritize development speed over security measures like encryption at rest and transit, secure authentication protocols, or proper access controls. Let me tell you: security breaches can sink an entire business overnight. Implementing robust security from day one ensures not only compliance but also gives users peace of mind.

#### **5. Performance Matters More Than Features**

While adding more features sounds appealing, remember that performance is where true customer satisfaction lies. Fast loading times, responsive interfaces, and efficient resource utilization make all the difference between delighting users versus frustrating them. Ensure each iteration focuses on improving overall performance before introducing additional bells and whistles.

#### **6. Customer Support Shouldn’t Be An Afterthought Either**

You think customers won't call? Think again! Every application has its quirks, bugs, and usage questions. Providing world-class support requires investing time upfront in crafting comprehensive documentation, setting up reliable issue tracking tools, and training your team to address complex queries efficiently. Don't underestimate the importance of excellent customer service!

#### **7. Scalability Is Key, But It Comes With Its Own Set Of Challenges**

Scaling an application may seem like the holy grail, but achieving it without encountering bottlenecks or complete system collapse is far easier said than done. Understand load balancing techniques, caching strategies, database design patterns, and distributed computing concepts. Remember, scalability doesn't happen magically; plan ahead and continually monitor performance metrics.

#### **8. Finally, Know That Iteration Over Perfection Wins The Day**

Last but certainly not least, don't fall prey to perfectionism.

Is it to accelerate sales, expand reach, or tap into new markets? **Thought #2: Choose Partners Wisely**

You can't force partnerships; they need to be mutually beneficial. Identify potential partners whose values align with yours and complement your strengths. **Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to today's discussion on the future of B2B marketing. My name is Jason Lemkin, and I'll be your host for this conversation.**

As we all know, the world of B2B marketing has undergone significant transformations over the past decade. From account-based marketing to content personalization, businesses have been experimenting with various strategies to reach their target audience.

But today, I want to talk about something that's going to change everything – AI agent recommendations. Yes, you heard me right! AI agents are no longer just chatbots; they're becoming intelligent advisors that can analyze customer behavior, preferences, and needs to provide personalized product or service suggestions.

The power of AI lies not only in its ability to process vast amounts of data but also in its capacity to learn from user interactions. By analyzing purchase history, browsing patterns, and search queries, AI agents can identify potential interests and make targeted recommendations. This approach enables customers to discover new products and services more efficiently than ever before.

Now, let's dive into some fascinating statistics:

* According to a recent study, 71% of consumers trust online reviews as much as personal recommendations.
* Another report reveals that 75% of users say they've bought a product after receiving an AI-powered recommendation.
* Meanwhile, sales teams using AI-driven tools experience up to 30% higher conversion rates compared to those relying solely on human intuition.

These numbers demonstrate the immense potential of AI agent recommendations in driving business growth. But here's the twist – AI agents play favorites!

When analyzing customer data, AI algorithms often favor certain profiles based on historical purchasing behavior, demographics, or other factors. While this might seem like a minor issue at first glance, it poses serious implications for marketers seeking to expand their reach beyond traditional customer segments.

To put it simply, if an AI agent consistently recommends products A, B, and C to a specific group, but rarely suggests D or E, we risk creating echo chambers where certain products remain underrepresented. Moreover, this dynamic reinforces existing biases within our customer base, potentially alienating underserved groups who may benefit from these alternative offerings.

So what does this mean for marketers? We need to develop more inclusive AI models that consider diverse perspectives, demographic nuances, and emerging trends. It's essential to ensure our AI agents don't become gatekeepers, limiting opportunities for innovative products and services.

In conclusion, the future of B2B marketing is indeed tied to AI agent recommendations. However, it's crucial to acknowledge the inherent bias within these systems. As we continue to explore the possibilities of AI, we must strive to create more equitable and representative platforms that empower both customers and businesses alike.

Thank you for joining me today, and I look forward to continuing this conversation in the comments below.

topic: You’re Lucky if Even 10% of Your Potential Customers are “In Market” At Any Given Time
prompt: Write a talk in the style of Jason Lemkin about: You’re Lucky if Even 10% of Your Potential Customers are “In Market” At Any Given Time
text:
**Lucky to Have 10%**

Hey everyone, it's Jason here from SaaStr. Today I want to talk about something that might seem counterintuitive at first but is actually super important for any B2B sales or marketing team out there.

You see, most people think they have this huge market out there waiting for them. They're convinced that every single one of their potential customers needs what they offer right now. But let me tell you a harsh truth - and I'm not sugarcoating it - you're lucky if even 10% of your potential customers are "in market" at any given time.

What do I mean by "in market"? Well, when someone says they need what we offer, that doesn't necessarily mean they can act on it today. In fact, research shows that only around 5-10% of all decision-makers are actively looking to buy something like our product at any point in time. That means the other 90-95% are either not interested yet, or they're too busy with more pressing priorities.

Now, before you start panicking and thinking, "But Jason, how am I supposed to grow my business if no one wants to buy?" Let me tell you - this isn't bad news! It just means you need to focus on those who are truly ready to make a purchase, rather than trying to convince everyone else.

Here's the thing: being aware of this reality changes everything. When you realize that your ideal customer base is much smaller than you thought, you can stop wasting resources on unqualified leads and instead go after those high-value prospects who will convert into paying customers.

So, what does this look like in practice? For us at SaaStr, it meant creating hyper-targeted content and messaging that spoke directly to our ideal customer segment. We stopped writing generic blog posts and started crafting detailed guides that addressed specific pain points and challenges faced by our target audience.

It also meant investing heavily in account-based marketing (ABM) efforts. We identified key accounts where our solution was particularly relevant, and then created personalized campaigns tailored specifically to each company's unique situation.

The results were staggering. Our conversion rates skyrocketed as we began targeting the right people with the right message at the right time.

Of course, none of this works unless you've got a deep understanding of your ideal customer's behavior, preferences, and buying habits. So take some time to really get inside their heads. Ask yourself:

* What keeps them up at night?
* What problems are they struggling to solve?
* Where do they hang out online?
* Who influences their purchasing decisions?

By answering these questions and tailoring your approach accordingly, you'll be amazed at how quickly you can turn 1% or 5% of your total addressable market into actual revenue-generating customers.

And remember - success in B2B sales and marketing comes down to three things: relevance, timing, and personalization. Focus on delivering value to your best-fit customers, reach them at exactly the moment they need it, and tailor your pitch to resonate with their unique concerns and motivations.

That's the secret sauce behind achieving explosive growth and turning a tiny fraction of your would-be customers into loyal advocates for life. Thanks for tuning in, folks!

---

**Scaling to $3 Billion: The Journey of Clio**

[ Slide - Title slide: "Clio - A $3 Billion SaaS Powerhouse" ]

As many of you know, Clio is not just any ordinary law practice management software company. They're on a mission to revolutionize the way lawyers work, leveraging cutting-edge technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to create a seamless experience for their customers.

So let's dive into the story of how they got here.

[ Slide - Founding Story ]

Jack and his co-founder, Rian Gomes, started Clio back in 2007. Their initial goal was simple: build a better tool for solo practitioners and small law firms to manage their cases more efficiently. But over time, they realized that there was so much more potential beyond just practice management.

They began experimenting with new features, integrating AI-powered tools, and building an ecosystem around their platform. And this is where things get really interesting.

Secondly, **innovation**, driven by a willingness to experiment and take calculated risks. From AI-powered document review to integrations with other industry-leading tools, Clio continuously pushes the boundaries of what's possible.

And thirdly, **a customer-centric approach**. By listening intently to its users and incorporating feedback into product development, Clio built trust and loyalty among its client base – which ultimately fueled rapid expansion.

text:

But fast forward just a few years later, and mobile gaming had become a whole new ball game. New companies like Supercell were popping up left and right, raking in millions from their hit titles.
